clue.text: Who made this old beast? O bursar, not us !

indicators.note: the question asks who made the beast, and the reply's letters are what it was made from, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks who created a prehistoric creature, and a college bursar protests that it was not their doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made' signals the anagram: the twelve letters of O BURSAR NOT US are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The great sauropod dinosaur is a long-extinct, ancient creature.

clue.text: Rough wood isn't good business

definitions.note: a clause where the answer is a noun: the phrase means an unfair transaction, which is not good business

parts.note: raw means rough or unrefined
deal is sawn pine or fir timber

explanation.surface: A complaint that selling unfinished timber is unprofitable.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAL is fir or pine planking, a usage common in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfair bargain or harsh treatment is the opposite of a fair transaction.

clue.text: Peary got there first

parts.note: the American explorer Robert Peary claimed in 1909 to be the first to reach the top of the world

explanation.surface: A historical claim about the explorer Peary's priority.
explanation.walkthrough: Peary's 1909 expedition claimed the Arctic's goal at the earth's axis.
explanation.definitionFit: The point at the earth's northern axis is where Peary's party claimed to arrive before anyone.

clue.text: Confused Irish tongue put over round it

definitions.text: Confused Irish tongue put over round it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a confused word has its letters mixed up, so the language name is jumbled

parts.note: Erse is an old name for Irish Gaelic

explanation.surface: Muddled Gaelic wrapped up somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' turns ERSE into SEER, placed below OVER in this down light. No separate definition is printed; one 'put over' others is a supervisor.
explanation.definitionFit: A supervisor is someone placed in charge above workers, set over them to watch their work.

clue.text: Lupin that flourished in a story

definitions.text: Lupin that flourished in a story

parts.words: Lupin that flourished in a story
parts.note: Maurice Leblanc's gentleman thief is the Frenchman Lupin, hero of many stories, not the garden plant

explanation.surface: A garden lupin that thrived in some tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lupin' looks like the flower, and 'flourished' supports that; it is the surname of Leblanc's fictional burglar.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename of Leblanc's French gentleman-burglar, who thrived in a long run of tales.

clue.text: Ben Ezra, perhaps

parts.note: Browning's poem title names a medieval Jewish scholar with his religious title before his name

explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning's poem 'Rabbi Ben Ezra' supplies the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham ibn Ezra was a Jewish teacher and scholar, so he bore the title of a religious teacher.

clue.text: Labour with a black suit -

parts.note: spades are a black card suit and also digging tools, and digging is the dull groundwork of a project

explanation.surface: Toiling while dressed in dark clothes, or a politician in mourning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' suggests clothing, but it is the card suit of spades; work with spades is digging, hence preparatory toil.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard preliminary groundwork is likened to digging, the toil of a gardener's tool shared with the card suit.

clue.text: If such malice goes to war it becomes a ship

definitions.text: If such malice goes to war it becomes a ship

parts.words: If such malice goes to war it becomes a ship
parts.note: the Royal Navy gave its destroyers names built on words for ill will, so this malice, gone to war, is a fighting vessel

explanation.surface: Bitterness taken to battle turns into a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Add -FUL or -FIRE and the word becomes HMS Spiteful or HMS Spitfire, both Royal Navy warships.
explanation.definitionFit: Malice and ill will are synonyms of the word, whose longer forms named Royal Navy fighting vessels.

clue.text: The daughter who went with the ducats

definitions.text: The daughter who went with the ducats

parts.words: The daughter who went with the ducats
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice Shylock's daughter elopes with Lorenzo, taking her father's money

explanation.surface: A girl who ran off with gold coins.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock laments 'My daughter! O my ducats!' when she elopes in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's moneylender's child eloped carrying his gold coins, so she is the girl described.

clue.text: Cryptically a result of one of those electricity cuts

definitions.text: Cryptically a result of one of those electricity cuts

parts.words: Cryptically a result of one of those electricity cuts
parts.note: a power cut leaves you with less power; read split, the word says exactly that, and as one word it means helpless

explanation.surface: A grumble about a household left in the dark by a blackout.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as POWER LESS, the word describes what a cut leaves you with; as a whole it means unable to act.
explanation.definitionFit: During a blackout the home has no electrical supply, and anyone lacking strength or authority is likewise without force.

clue.text: It seems a vehicle for stopping rather than going

definitions.text: It seems a vehicle for stopping rather than going

parts.words: It seems a vehicle for stopping rather than going
parts.note: the word names both an old horse-drawn carriage and the device on a wheel that slows it, so a vehicle that sounds made for halting

explanation.surface: A wry remark about a car that seems built to halt rather than travel.
explanation.walkthrough: A brake was an open horse-drawn carriage, so the word is a vehicle, yet its everyday meaning is the stopping device.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an old carriage for travel and the mechanism that slows wheels, hence the paradox.

clue.text: One puts a bit between them in more senses than one

definitions.text: One puts a bit between them in more senses than one

parts.words: One puts a bit between them in more senses than one
parts.note: a horse's bit sits in the mouth, and a bit of food is also put there to chew

explanation.surface: A rider bridling a horse, or someone taking a mouthful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit' works both as the metal mouthpiece for a horse and as a morsel of food; both go between the same pair of rows in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a bridle's mouthpiece and a mouthful are placed between the rows of biting enamel in the jaws.

clue.text: Ten less in these maybe

definitions.note: the pronoun points back to the answer itself, the guards being described

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters of these three words could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A puzzling count: there might be ten fewer of some group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' signals the anagram of TEN LESS IN; 'these' stands for the answer, a setter's habit of the era rather than a true definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names guards on watch, the people 'these' refers to in the clue.

clue.text: A mistake in the garden

definitions.meaning: a howler or blunder, in British slang
a plant that flowers, as found in a garden bed

explanation.surface: An error made while gardening.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a bloomer is a gaffe; literally it is any plant that blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both slang for a blunder and a description of anything flowering among the beds.

clue.text: Appropriately like Leander's achievement

parts.note: in Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to his lover Hero, a brave feat done for Hero

explanation.surface: Praise for the swim of the Greek lover in legend.
explanation.walkthrough: The swim was brave, and it was done for Hero, so the adjective is apt in two ways: hence 'Appropriately'.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossing the strait each night was a bold, courageous deed, and its purpose was the priestess named Hero.

clue.text: Argue once (anag)

indicators.note: the setter labels the clue as an anagram outright, so these two words are rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints no definition: '(anag)' says only that ARGUE ONCE is rearranged, leaving the crossings to confirm the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means to hearten or spur on, a sense the clue leaves for the solver to supply.

clue.text: It helps one to get a good spread

definitions.text: It helps one to get a good spread

parts.words: It helps one to get a good spread
parts.note: a spread sounds like a feast, but this is a flat-bladed tool for spreading butter or paste

explanation.surface: Something that helps produce a lavish meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' suggests a fine banquet, but means smearing a soft substance evenly.
explanation.definitionFit: A broad flexible blade is used to smear things evenly across a surface.

clue.text: This, perhaps, is what is told, by dandelion clocks

definitions.text: This, perhaps, is what is told, by dandelion clocks

parts.words: This, perhaps, is what is told, by dandelion clocks
parts.note: children blow at a dandelion's fluffy head to tell the hour, and the puffs scatter the plant's seeds

explanation.surface: Children telling the hour by blowing on dandelion heads.
explanation.walkthrough: A dandelion clock is the seed head; the game tells the time by counting puffs, and what it really marks is the season of sowing.
explanation.definitionFit: The season for sowing is when seeds disperse, which the fluffy heads mark as they scatter.

clue.text: A boat tied up

definitions.meaning: a ... boat carried mail and passengers on a regular route
a parcel or bundle wrapped and tied with string

explanation.surface: A vessel moored at the quayside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tied up' reads as mooring, but it is the second sense: a small wrapped parcel.
explanation.definitionFit: A mail steamer on a fixed run was so called, and the word also names a small wrapped parcel.

clue.text: Where "we buried him darkly at dead of night

definitions.text: Where "we buried him darkly at dead of night

parts.words: Where "we buried him darkly at dead of night
parts.note: the line is from Charles Wolfe's poem on Sir John Moore, buried at the Spanish port after the 1809 battle

explanation.surface: A quotation asking where a soldier was secretly buried.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir John Moore fell in 1809 at the battle at A Coruña in Spain and was buried there at night.
explanation.definitionFit: The British name for the Galician port of A Coruña, scene of Moore's death and night burial.

clue.text: Tea and cake

explanation.surface: An afternoon snack on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words simply join, and the whole clue also describes the bun, eaten toasted at teatime.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sweet yeast bun served at the afternoon meal, so both words describe it.

clue.text: A dish for a salt, but surely salt itself

definitions.text: A dish for a salt, but surely salt itself

parts.words: A dish for a salt, but surely salt itself
parts.note: a salt is a sailor; sailors ate a layered meat-and-crust stew of this name, yet its first half already means the briny ocean

explanation.surface: A sailor's meal that ought to be salty in itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'salt' is first an old sailor, then seawater: the dish's name begins with the word for the briny deep.
explanation.definitionFit: A layered meat stew under pastry crust was a traditional shipboard meal for sailors.

clue.text: It's simply senseless

parts.note: an adjective for something silly, empty and pointless

explanation.surface: An exasperated verdict on a foolish plan.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means silly, empty or pointless, a synonym of witless.

clue.text: A sign for swordsmen

parts.note: a dummy head in Ottoman style was the target that cavalrymen cut at in sword drill, and also a common inn sign

explanation.surface: An inn board hung outside for fencers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Turk's Head was a frequent pub sign, and the same name was given to the target head used in British cavalry sword practice.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure painted on many inn boards was also what troopers aimed their blades at in drill.

clue.text: A crooked shoot, that's true enough

definitions.note: the archaic adjective for real or genuine, as in 'in sooth'

indicators.note: a crooked thing is bent out of shape, so the word shoot is twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A bent sapling, and someone conceding that's right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crooked' signals the anagram of SHOOT.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for real or genuine, surviving in 'soothsayer', a teller of truth.

clue.text: It could be put on for Sinclair

definitions.note: the American novelist Sinclair, author of The Jungle, had this first name

indicators.note: could be suggests these letters might become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: Something that might be worn or staged on behalf of a man called Sinclair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' signals the anagram of PUT ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist of The Jungle bore this forename before his surname Sinclair.

clue.text: Asking for more tobacco ?

definitions.meaning: Dickens's workhouse orphan Oliver famously asks 'Please, sir, I want some more'
a ... roll of tobacco leaf for chewing or pipe smoking

explanation.surface: A smoker wanting another pipeful.
explanation.walkthrough: Dickens's orphan Oliver asks for more gruel; the same word names a rope of tobacco leaf.
explanation.definitionFit: The orphan who asked for more bore this surname, and a coiled roll of leaf goes by the same name.

clue.text: Such crude language

parts.note: a jargon or uncouth dialect, a dismissive word for foreign or unfamiliar speech

explanation.surface: A disapproving reaction to swearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crude' suggests swearing, but the word means a rough, outlandish tongue or jargon.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang term is a dismissive name for unfamiliar speech or jargon, a rough sort of tongue.

clue.text: The result of a very important person getting wrong with his food

indicators.note: a person getting things wrong muddles them, so these letters are jumbled together

parts.note: VIP is short for very important person
a ration is a person's allotted share of food

explanation.surface: A dignitary who is served the wrong meal ends up going hungry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting wrong' jumbles VIP and RATION together; the definition leans on the rest of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardship and want are what follows from being badly fed, so the outcome is lack of necessities.

clue.text: Even matches I make of these

definitions.note: the pronoun points back to the answer itself, the feats being described

indicators.note: the speaker makes something new out of these words, so their letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A sportsman boasting that drawn games count as successes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make of' signals the anagram of EVEN MATCHES I; 'these' stands for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Feats and accomplishments are what the pronoun refers to, the things the speaker counts as successes.
